The command-line style interface makes you feel like you're really in the chair, feeding intel and solving cases under pressure. Every mission kept me hooked, and the writing is surprisingly sharp.

Only gripe? I wish it were longer, and the lack of manual saves can be frustrating. Still, for fans of immersive puzzle games and narrative-driven experiences, this one’s a hidden gem.

8.5/10 – Highly recommend.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 98:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆ (8/10)

[i] The Operator [/i] casts you not as a hero in the field, but as the analyst—the voice behind the computer—supporting agents from the shadows. It’s a fascinating setup and a fresh twist on crime-solving games, and usually almost always lives up to its potential!

🖥[b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] Authentic "operator" fantasy. You monitor missions from your desk, field phone calls, look through mysterious documents, and scrub through CCTV footage. 

[*] Diverse tools. The game gives you a chem scanner, facial recognition database, image enhancement tech, and document search systems. For example, in one mission, you identify a suspect by cross-referencing a blurry security camera with an equally blurry security footage of his car and license plate. That kind of detective work feels cool. You feel smart when it works.

[*] Great use of puzzles under pressure. A standout moment has you guiding a field agent through bomb defusal. You have to analyze chemicals, check your reference files, and read out step-by-step instructions—all while the timer ticks down. These time-sensitive missions are where the game shines.

[*] Well-done audio design. The UI clicks, radio static, and phone calls all contribute to a grounded, late-'90s thriller vibe. The voice acting is low-key but sells the scenario well, especially during moments of stress or confusion.

[*] No filler. It’s tight and focused. No wandering, no padding. You’re thrown into the action quickly and missions move at a brisk pace.
[/list]

[b]🧾 Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*] Flat characters. The field agents and mysterious hacker HAL are more archetypes than flesh-and-blood. They push the story forward, but rarely surprise

[*] Choices don’t matter much. There are dialogue branches, but most are cosmetic. Whether you’re professional or snarky, or even whether you succeed or fail at certain puzzles, the game mostly funnels you into the same story beats.

[*] Abrupt ending. The game ends just as things get interesting. HAL’s storyline ramps up, then vanishes. You barely get to dig into the conspiracy or see the consequences of your actions. It feels like a miniseries that ends on episode three.
[/list]
[hr]

review_text_raw:
Firstly, I'd like to preface my review, by saying if you are interested in this game. Do not watch a play through of it, try the demo, see if your engaged and then buy the game. This review is spoiler free.

A lovely crafted indie detective thriller, with a fantastic narrative story provided me with a very enjoyable and gripping 3/4 hours of game play on my first play through. The game has been painstakingly crafted down to every individual element, and it really shows, but this love creates a gripping, edge of your seat experience which will make you truly engage with every character and feel every emotion in a short space of time. The time setting is fantastic, blending a feel of early 2000 technology, with modern software and interface feel. When the game says use headphones, I usually disagree. But this is one of the rare examples which playing with headphones or a decent speaker set-up takes this from a game to a true experience.

The game has got an excellent blend of mixed media, cinematic and a truly atmospheric score that intertwines with the narrative in a beautiful way to create this experience. Throughout the game it makes you constantly think, am I making the right choices, is this how I solve this puzzle, and gives you everything you need to figure these out in a well executed manner without holding your hand too much. Even the achievements have been carefully thought out to provide you just enough information that your inquisitive brain wants to fully unravel and unlock each one.

Do I wish the game was longer? Yes. Am I disappointing by this? No, I loved every second of my playtime and strongly look forward to what the developer and his talented contributors bring next. Would I consider buying a future DLC expansion? Easily, this has been the most engaged with a game I've been for a very long time, and I would love to see what the developer brings to the operative universe next. 

This game is truly, one of those rare indie gems, that brings the passion and story into an over saturated gaming market, and really makes you wish more development companies (Especially AAA) had the same mentality and craft.

review_text_raw:
The Operator, developed by Bureau 81 and published by Bureau 81 together with indienova, is a tightly focused narrative puzzle game that transforms the quiet, procedural work of intelligence analysis into a tense and engaging thriller. Rather than placing players in the role of an action hero or field agent, the game casts them as a desk-bound operator, someone whose power comes not from physical presence but from information, observation, and deduction. This shift in perspective defines the entire experience, creating a game that feels intimate, cerebral, and deliberately restrained.

You play as Evan Tanner, a newly recruited operator working for the fictional Federal Department of Intelligence. Your job is to support agents in the field by analysing data, processing evidence, and drawing connections that others might miss. The game unfolds almost entirely through Evan’s workstation, presented as a simulated computer desktop filled with databases, analysis tools, messaging systems, and case files. This interface-driven approach immediately sets the tone: instead of cinematic spectacle, The Operator relies on immersion through routine, making the player feel like they are genuinely sitting at a government terminal late at night, piecing together fragments of truth.

Gameplay revolves around solving a series of cases that gradually escalate in complexity and importance. Early tasks feel procedural—identifying suspects, tracing movements, or cross-referencing records—but as the story unfolds, patterns begin to emerge and the stakes rise. Players are required to closely read documents, examine photos and videos, search databases, and interpret subtle clues hidden in plain sight. The puzzles reward attentiveness and logical reasoning, often asking players to synthesize information from multiple sources rather than relying on a single obvious answer. When a breakthrough occurs, it feels earned, the result of careful thought rather than trial and error.

As the narrative progresses, the game shifts from isolated casework into a broader conspiracy. A mysterious hacker begins to interfere with FDI systems, raising questions about surveillance, authority, and the reliability of the information you’re working with. This transition adds narrative tension without abandoning the game’s grounded tone. The story remains largely linear, but it is effectively paced, allowing suspense to build gradually as seemingly unrelated assignments reveal deeper connections. Dialogue and character interactions are understated, delivered through calls, messages, and system prompts rather than dramatic cutscenes, which reinforces the feeling that you are always working behind the scenes.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is how convincingly it uses its interface as both a storytelling and gameplay tool. Every window, search bar, and analysis program feels purposeful, and learning how to use these tools becomes part of the experience. While some mechanics are simplified or exaggerated for gameplay purposes, they remain believable within the fiction, maintaining immersion. The design encourages players to slow down, double-check assumptions, and think critically—mistakes often stem from overlooking details rather than misunderstanding mechanics.

Visually, The Operator embraces a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic inspired by older operating systems and institutional software. The interface is dense but readable, intentionally lacking visual flair in favor of authenticity. This design choice may feel dry to some players, but it suits the game’s themes perfectly, emphasizing bureaucracy, control, and the monotony of surveillance work. Subtle audio cues, ambient hums, and restrained music enhance tension without distracting from concentration, allowing the player’s focus to remain on the task at hand.

In terms of pacing, the game strikes a careful balance. It is compact, typically completed in a handful of hours, but it avoids feeling rushed. Each case builds naturally on the last, and the increasing narrative weight keeps momentum strong. The linear structure limits replayability, as choices rarely branch into significantly different outcomes, but this also allows the developers to maintain tight narrative control and deliver a coherent, focused story without filler.

Community reception reflects appreciation for the game’s originality and execution. Players who enjoy detective work, mystery narratives, and “games on a computer” style experiences frequently praise its atmosphere and puzzle design. Criticism tends to focus on its short length, limited player agency, and occasional moments where immersion is broken by game-like constraints. Even so, these issues rarely overshadow the strengths of the experience, particularly for players aligned with its intended audience.

Taken as a whole, The Operator is a confident and distinctive narrative puzzle game that finds tension in observation rather than action. It succeeds by committing fully to its premise, turning data analysis and desk work into compelling gameplay through thoughtful design and strong thematic focus. While it may not appeal to players seeking open-ended systems or high replay value, it offers a memorable, tightly constructed experience for those who enjoy slow-burn storytelling, logical deduction, and the quiet unease of uncovering truths from behind a screen.

Rating: 9/10

review_text_raw:
[h1][b] TLDR: Sells itself as an investigative puzzler but delivers a mostly on-rails visual novel experience. The handful of genuine puzzles are great, making their scarcity all the more frustrating.
[/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Neat investigative puzzles (ENHANCE….ENHANCE)
➕Some nice puzzles, like bomb defuse

[h1]NEUTRALS: [/h1]
🔹Story is good, but a bit too on-rails and hand-holding

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Lots of unskippable intentionally blurry cutscenes leaves a cheap or vague feeling
➖Some reveals are not as big as they should be simply because you wouldn’t know things that your character would know

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely from a computer screen and is set in the 90s, we’re talking older CRT monitor screens. There’s not much exploration to be found, as you work for the government and everything is pretty locked down. I’d say the world is a bit basic and simple, only serving as a UI to show some puzzles. 

The narrative has some good parts. You play as Evan Tanner, a Federal Department of Investigation (FDI) operator, in which your job is to assist field agents. You very quickly learn that there’s something going on and you are enlisted, whether you want to or not, to uncover the truth. 
So while I did enjoy the story to an extent, any scene not at the computer and is told through a characters eyes is a blurry mess of objects that are nearly undecipherable. This could be something related to the story, but I don’t want to give the game the benefit of the doubt here and say that it worsens the experience. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The gameplay seems pretty cool at first, but you quickly realize how on-rails the game is. Essentially, this is a glorified visual novel with a few puzzles sprinkled in. At first, I felt like Garcia from Criminal Minds - I was the internet sleuth assisting agents in the field by giving them on-the-fly information to help with cases. But unfortunately, the game isn’t as cool as that. 
The loop consists of you having a conversation, being presented with evidence, and then using the 2-3 tools at your disposal to answer a question presented by the conversation. For example, you’ll need to identify a killer and a victim by scanning their faces to get their names, then look them up in the FDI database. Same thing with licenses plates or analyzing footage/pictures. It does sound very cool, but I can’t emphasize enough the on-rails experience and lack of deep puzzle mechanics. This is more of a game focused on the narrative. 

The difficulty is forgiving. I’m pretty sure I made every wrong choice in the game, yet still made it to the end. I literally messed up a [spoiler]bomb defuse and got an agent killed[/spoiler]. Whoops. Despite these consequences, this doesn’t seem like it impacted the game as much and wasn’t mentioned again other than a few brief times after the fact. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Being that the game is from the point of view of a computer screen and all “Real” scenes are a blurry mess, I’d say the quality isn’t great. What footage you do see is grainy 90’s-era quality, but aside from that the computer UI is good and crisp. 

On the technical side, I had no issues, encountered no bugs, and ran the game without issues. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The music isn’t really noticeable, but it does increase in intensity during high-drama parts. 

There is a lot of voice acting, and it all sounds good. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [2/10] [/b] [/h1]
Not a lot of replay value here, unless you want to redo the puzzles again for achievements. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The Operator is described as a game with detective/investigation, and puzzle elements. I’d estimate the game to be about 70% story/narrative focus, 20% puzzles, and 10% deducing or investigating. I’d say that Operator is an okay game, but I was a bit disappointed by the mystery and investigative sides. This is very much a visual novel game more than anything, and as someone that likes visual novels, I was expecting more to use my brain to make deductions instead of clicking pre-defined replies. 

The game does have a few puzzles. I’d say maybe ~10 at the most, and despite that small number, I found them to be good puzzles. Analyzing gunpowder was really cool. Defusing a bomb on the fly was also great. If the game was more focused on gameplay like that, then I’d give it a much higher score, but these are the highest highs that The Operator offers, and there’s only a few of them. 

The real focus of the game is on the narrative. While I wouldn’t consider the narrative to be bad, there were a few parts that were either ridiculously obvious, or a missed opportunity. 
Obvious, because of metagaming - anyone who watches mystery shows knows that there’s only so many characters who could be the culprit due to you the show introducing them to the viewer. Same concept here, it’s obviously going to be the handful of people you know about already. 
Missed opportunity because you as the player only know what you know. One part in particular [spoiler]has the player finding out his apartment is being watched with a camera, and you have to identify whose apartment it is[/spoiler]. Well how can you possibly figure that out without knowing anything about the characters' life, nor ever having been there? Dumb. 

Overall, I do recommend The Operator, but it’s important that you know what you’re going into. This is NOT about deduction or investigating, and that’s not necessarily a bad thing, but I feel the game presents itself in a way that it’s something that it isn’t. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$14 base price is a bit much for a ~5 hour game with very low replay value. Wait for a sale. Around ~$5-7 would be a good point.

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1] The Operator is described as a game with detective/investigation, and puzzle elements. I’d estimate the game to be about 70% story/narrative focus, 20% puzzles, and 10% deducing or investigating. I’d say that Operator is an okay game, but I was a bit disappointed by the mystery and investigative sides. This is very much a visual novel game more than anything, and as someone that likes visual novels, I was expecting more to use my brain to make deductions instead of clicking pre-defined replies. The game does have a few puzzles. I’d say maybe ~10 at the most, and despite that small number, I found them to be good puzzles. Analyzing gunpowder was really cool. Defusing a bomb on the fly was also great. If the game was more focused on gameplay like that, then I’d give it a much higher score, but these are the highest highs that The Operator offers, and there’s only a few of them. The real focus of the game is on the narrative. While I wouldn’t consider the narrative to be bad, there were a few parts that were either ridiculously obvious, or a missed opportunity. Obvious, because of metagaming - anyone who watches mystery shows knows that there’s only so many characters who could be the culprit due to you the show introducing them to the viewer. Same concept here, it’s obviously going to be the handful of people you know about already. Missed opportunity because you as the player only know what you know. Well how can you possibly figure that out without knowing anything about the characters' life, nor ever having been there? Dumb. Overall, I do recommend The Operator, but it’s important that you know what you’re going into. I grade The Operator A-. This is an excellent investigation game with a great premise and fantastic presentation, including the music. While it doesn't have Hollywood-style hacking, given that its setting is in 1992 and you're working in a government alphabet agency, the developers nailed the look and feel of a stripped down government UI. Even right down to a part where you use an even [i]older[/i] computer and the visual area changes from 16:9 to 4:3. Nice touch.

The story is very well written. I didn't detect a single typo or weird turn of phrase. A lot of detective games here on Steam are made by non-English developers, and so they tend to get wonky in localization. The Operator does not have that issue. The story is almost entirely logical and internally consistent, and it was fun to experience.

The only thing is the story's wheels fell off at the very end. While the story beats and twists were a bit obvious, the final hard twist -- though it was presented really well -- makes absolutely no logical sense even within the context of the world that is presented to us. I come away from it with a lot more questions, but not the good "What are they going to do next?" kind. It's more the "Why did the basic premise happen in the first place?" kind. Unless there was some subtlety I missed, I can think of a thousand reasons why the first step of the plot shouldn't have happened, and that sort of makes the ending a little bit of a letdown.

But don't let that dissuade you. I'm happy to have bought the game and supported the developer, especially because the gameplay was excellent. I really enjoyed the act of investigating as a government agent and having tools like face-scanning and an omni-database just a mouse click away. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy games with hacking -- whether Hollwood hacking like Orwell or more script-based hacking like HackNet -- but it was really fun to be an agent for the "other side" and just have some improbable tools at my fingertips. If there is a sequel, while I hope the writing makes a little more logical sense, I really encourage the devs to keep the gameplay just as it is.

review_text_raw:
The Operator — Quick Review

Platform: PC (Steam)

Genre: Puzzle / Simulation / Mystery

Verdict: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ A standout puzzle experience

---

What It Is

The Operator puts you in the role of a remote operator—essentially a digital detective working through cases from behind a screen. You dig through databases, analyze evidence, make phone calls, and piece together mysteries using a realistic desktop interface. It's the kind of game that makes you feel like you're actually doing the job.

Why It Works

The puzzle design is the star. The game doesn't hold your hand. You're given tools, a case file, and just enough rope to figure things out yourself. The satisfaction of connecting two pieces of evidence you found hours apart is genuinely rewarding. It respects your intelligence in a way few puzzle games do.

The interface feels authentic. The fake desktop OS, the clunky database searches, the phone calls—it all adds to the immersion. You're not just solving puzzles; you're inhabiting a role.

The layered structure keeps it fresh. Each case builds on what you've learned, but introduces new mechanics or twists so it never feels repetitive. By the time you've played "a couple layers" (as you put it), the game has opened up into something much deeper than it first appears.

The Vibe

It's methodical. Deliberate. If you want fast-paced action, this isn't it. But if you enjoy the slow burn of untangling a mystery—cross-referencing names, verifying alibis, catching contradictions—The Operator is incredibly satisfying.

Bottom Line

One of the better puzzle experiences on Steam right now. It trusts the player, delivers great "aha!" moments, and wraps it in a polished, believable package. Highly recommended if you enjoy games like Papers, Please, Orwell, or Return of the Obra Dinn.

TL;DR: This game is a 3-hour long visual novel with not-that-meaningful choices, good music and sound effects, narration, and an interesting but short linear story line. 0 replay-ability.

The nice things:

[spoiler]1. The cutscenes where the game shows you that time has passed is nice. The subtle drug-taking noises and coughing noises makes a good addition. Even though there is no real graphics here, it shows that the developers put in a lot of efforts in making the game immersive.
2. The interface and UI, especially the keyboard noises you make when you are typing, makes me reminiscent of a time when I wasn't even alive. It just feels nice to type things and click on things.
3. Narration is good, not crazy impressive, but good. That's a hard bar to pass by my standards.

review_text_raw:
(This review contains information that might be considered spoilers for some, so read with caution!)

TL; DR:
It holds your hand throughout the game. The investigative puzzles are immersive, but simple and provides very little challenge. It's short, but you might possible still like it for it's presentation and story. If there was a "lukewarm" rating, I would pick that. But since it's clearly a labor of love, I'm inclined to rate positively.

The longer review:

When I heard of The Operator a few days before launch, I was hoping for something to scratch that Obra Dinn / Curse of the Golden Idol itch. Not very many games manage to make you feel like a proper investigator or makes you feel super clever when you progress, and those two games are the gold standard.

The Operator - unfortunately - is not that game.

The immersion is great. You definitely feel like an operator, scanning photos for details that you then input into various databases to yield result. The interface is exactly how you'd imagine a 90's 'hacker' terminal to look like, complete with a terminal and an official looking 'FBI' interface. The majority of the game is fully voiced with competent actors (for the budget).

Although a very polished and - for its medium - a cinematic experience, gameplay-wise it falls into many of the same pitfalls as other "investigative" games like it. The puzzles are - for the most part, but with notable exceptions - simple, requiring few steps to solve. Your hand is woefully held through each of them and the freedom to make your own deductions are sorely lacking. For the most part the tools required to solve a certain puzzle will appear when needed, and disappear when not needed anymore.

The story is decent and very on-par for such a game. It doesn't fully manage to suck you into the world, however. For one, the main plot felt rushed. You're a new operator working cases, and the very first case you receive is a part of a brewing conspiracy. Every case following that is connected in some way. In my opinion, the game doesn't take it's time to build up the world or the characters before placing you front and center into the main plot thread. 

Some of the major plot twists are extremely predictable, and some of what is presented as a major plot development honestly really isn't. We don't know the involved characters enough to care when the revelation is given to us.
The game also makes the cardinal sin of ending abruptly with no real resolution, most questions left unanswered and a feeling that your actions throughout the game had little impact.

A lot of this comes down to personal tastes, hopes and expectations, however. Chances are you'll like this game for it's good presentation and decent enough puzzles. It's not particularly expensive (though maybe a bit pricey for the estimated game time).

So here's a recent and what I consider accurate short review.

The game is worth playing and given it's a bit over the length of a regular movie maybe 2 I'd say at the price of 15 - 25 it's reasonable given movie ticket and popcorn. Replay value isn't really there unless you forget what happened and replay a few years later, but who knows!

It's not really an investigation game and while I'm fine with linear games it is important to mention the plot largely is linear and the actions you can take are too. It's generous with the help in most cases too. It's more like an interactable movie from the main interface of a computer.

The plot and such isn't anything too crazy if you've seen Bourne and Mission Impossible and stuff like that, but it's a pretty good one.

The bomb segment is probably the best part, but it is an absolutely shame that the defusal process is NOT random but instead always the same thing. They had so much information for alternative bombs after all. The ending is highly depressing and ultimately doesn't make a lot of sense due to the wiping the servers and such. I think it should have kept that held back for a potential sequel.

I'd of liked more investigation options, more possibilities to really need to assess things. But I would be interested in a sequel or another game expanding on the systems.

Is it worth a purchase? Yes. And it does really good job at being voluminous in the details and subject matter that they're going into, sometimes a bit too confusingly haha. Whether that's technobabble or someone knew what they were writing about is hard to say. And the voice acting is solid too.

Makes no sense the agents don't have a partner with them at all times tho.

--- I recommend this purchase as a story focused gamer.
Other games you might want to consider that I've played recently that are also story focused or just good: Escape Simulator, Hades, Operation Tango, 	The Operator (this one), Roottree (tho it's less like a game), StarCraft 2 especially Legacy, We Were Here series sequels (but it can be hard at times), Ixion, Strange Horticulture, and a few others.

Thanks for reading --- February 2025.

Edit: As a side note, while the developer seems very pleased with its soundtrack there were a lot of times I didn't really hear any music going on which seemed a bit odd, like during the first server room pursuit to reveal some data.

I want to give this an honest review, because although I enjoyed it and the game does have a lot of potential, there are some setbacks to it as well.

Positives:
-The gameplay is fun and paced well. It never felt boring or slow, and the storyline was intriguing and kept me interested throughout.
-The detective work was interesting, but not too challenging. Other than [spoiler] the bomb defusing puzzle which was super annoying and convoluted out of nowhere and with a time limit that made it even worse [/spoiler] I could progress easily without feeling like it was too simple.
-The game's ui was easy to use and had nice to look at.

Negatives:
-It's well written, but really short. As you can tell from my playtime, it moved super quickly. While the story was still satisfying for the most part, it felt like it ended prematurely due to the short length. I would have liked to have seen at least a few more days worth of gameplay.
-The ending felt, to me, very unsatisfying. [spoiler] Although I'm sure, given the after credits scene, this is meant to be a cliff hanger for the next game, the way it ended just left me feeling like all the work I had done was meaningless and therefore the game had been meaningless. That's not to say the ending was all bad or should be completely changed. But, for example, if it had ended with one person being apprehended, or something similar to give some sense of conclusion, it would have been a lot better. As it is, I finished it somewhat annoyed. As if I had wasted all that effort for no reward, and an unfinished storyline. [/spoiler] This criticism is somewhat of a personal opinion, I know, but it really soured my view of the game at the end. Which was a shame, because up until that very moment I was super engrossed in the story and really enjoying it.

Overall, I enjoyed the gameplay and story right up until the final minute. So I would recommend the game, if you got it on sale or don't mind that it is very short, and you aren't put off by the thought of an abrupt ending. I think this studio did a great job producing it though and telling a story, and look forward to their next game. I only hope their next ending will feel a bit more satisfying for the player.

review_text_raw:
I did enjoy The Operator, but it's very much one of those titles I wish I could give a sideways thumb to. I can't explain why without spoilers, so I'll tag that section.

This is one of those games that takes place entirely in menus, but still manages to have a compelling story with some puzzling that keeps you engaged in relatively simple game play systems by making you use the analytical parts of your brain. Taking place in a fictional early 1990s where people have cell phones and wireless Internet access, you're playing as a remote operator at the Not FBI who is tasked with helping field agents analyze data relevant to their cases. As you progress, you'll start to become embroiled in a huge conspiracy that goes through many elements of the agency and other places as well. The interface is nice, the music is good and the voice acting of the characters is actually great. If you like stuff that's more action focused, this might not be for you, but I was kept engaged throughout.

Non-specific spoilers and attached criticisms below:

[spoiler]Unfortunately, this game is really let down by it's in my opinion, pretty awful ending. Things come to a head very quickly and the conclusion is thrown at you over just a couple of minutes and isn't well paced. Things somehow manage to end on both a massive cliffhanger, but also very definitively, making the story unsatisfying and also not necessarily possible to continue in a sequel or expansion. You're introduced to some pretty cool investigative mechanics early on that only ever get used once and you also make many what seem like important choices, but you're given a very strong indication by the end that none of them ultimately mattered, nor impacted the outcome. People have said in the forums that there's little narrative value to additional playthroughs.

As a result, the story goes from intriguing and tense to being a big let down and feels like it was rushed and not fully planned out. This took an otherwise great experience and knocked a lot of wind out of its sails for me.

I still recommend this, but definitely on sale. I'm hoping that the developer puts out some content updates to expand the ending more, but I'm not expecting that.[/spoiler]

Overall enjoyable. Decent interface and storyline, good variety of puzzle mechanics, low to medium difficulty and complexity.

I'm usually not a fan of dialogue choices and multiple endings, so I didn't know how to feel when I found out this game [i]doesn't[/i] have alternative endings.  Like another user put it, it really felt like I had reached the "bad ending", and that I was supposed to make different choices.  But playing through a second time did not change the outcomes aside from slightly different dialogue, and seeing one or two subtle hints I had missed the first time around.

And the developer has confirmed that it's not intended to be replayable (see the dev's [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/1771980/discussions/0/4511002214535949429/]community post[/url])

The interface is quite well done, with a variety of technical mechanics.  The in-game documents and user manuals are quite impressively believable in style, while staying relevant to the gameplay, and to the storyline.  I quite enjoyed the [spoiler]"Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes"[/spoiler] style puzzle.

I was a little disappointed that the terminal was so limited, but given this is a relatively small game, that's understandable.

At times, especially at the start, it felt like a bit of information overwhelm moving too quickly, but it generally seems to be quite forgiving (though I haven't tested what happens if you don't answer a call, or fail to [spoiler]defuse the bomb[/spoiler]).

Often it felt a bit too heavy on the handholding.  [spoiler]The "watch me."  "Are you watching me?" prompts for the scripted surveillance made me giggle[/spoiler].  Most of the big reveals were heavily hinted at early on so I knew long before the characters themselves knew.  There were a couple that surprised me though.

The voice acting was quite good.  As was the sound design, and animations.  There's quite a few unskippable animations but they're generally done quite well and relevant to the storyline or puzzles.

Overall decent little game.  First playthrough took me just about under ~6hrs at a meandering pace (and not keeping track of breaks).  Would play a sequel if it's ever made.

I really don't know how to rate this game. If steam had a "Neutral" option i would have definitely selected that.
With the strict "Yes" or "No" system, I'll hesitantly go for a positive review.

Let's start with the good: It's a really fun game with an interesting story and really good gameplay. The puzzles were interesting and pretty creative. The voice acting was well done and the UI felt nice to use. 
Also, unlike most other games like this, this game does at least try to be accurate with it's technology. Some creative liberties are taken, but as a technically minded person I wasn't screaming "That's not how that works!" all the time.

Now for my main issue: This game is way too short for the price. The game took me 4 hours and that was without trying to go fast. If I tried I feel like this game could be 100% in less that 3 hours (maybe even <2h).
It's not a full $60 game, but even for $15 this is just too short. And the story ends right as it starts getting interesting. Right after some actual intrigue is revealed the credits roll.
Another issue is that it's very linear. It doesn't matter what you do, there is only a single ending. The different options only affect which 10 second response you'll get and nothing after that.

I don't think it's worth getting this game for the full price, but if it's for sale for <$10 it's an alright deal.

The Operator offers a remarkably engaging narrative experience, supported by a strong storyline and a well-executed plot twist. The structure of each case is thoughtfully designed: from the call system to the investigative tasks, every step feels purposeful and polished. Working through evidence, analyzing data, and piecing together conclusions is consistently satisfying and stands out as one of the game’s greatest strengths.

Because the investigative tools and the workstation interface are so enjoyable to use, I found myself wishing for a mode that would provide long-term engagement beyond the main story. The campaign can be completed relatively quickly, and once it ends, the gameplay loop—despite being excellent—comes to an abrupt stop.

A dedicated free-play or “ongoing operations” mode could meaningfully extend the game’s lifespan. For example, players could receive procedurally generated cases or scenario-based assignments that scale in complexity, allowing them to continue applying the tools and systems introduced in the main storyline. This would give players who enjoy the investigative process a space to keep refining their skills and exploring the mechanics without a fixed ending.

I am very much looking forward to The Operator 2, and I genuinely believe that adding an optional long-term mode—whether free-play, case generator, or rotating scenario board—would significantly enhance replay value and increase the game’s overall appeal.

For anyone considering this title: the core experience is absolutely worth it, and the investigative gameplay is exceptionally well-crafted. The story alone justifies the €14 price, and I can recommend it without hesitation.

As the developer says, it's a 3-4 hour experience with almost no replay value (unless you want a few missable achievements).

The plot is above average, the graphics are pretty solid, and the audio is well suited.

There are some teething pains, such as unskippable blurs that count as cutscenes and if you ever replay a section you'll be sitting through the exact same dialogue all over again. There's also some issues with clickable areas in some scenes and a certain technical scene being a little hard to parse, since the manual uses terminology that doesn't *quite* fit.

However, the experience was quite lovely. The technical implementation is far above average, with dynamic windows, active text scrolling, and audio cues when you scroll to a certain section of text. It's extremely well coded. I see a lot of Unity games with UI issues, but this was as solid an implementation as I've seen. Well thought out, well executed, marvelous job!

And the amount of effort for a single dev, even with the support provided, is astonishing. Making this in *only* three years is quite impressive.

I do wish it was a more dynamic experience, but that requires an astonishing amount of work. As a stepping stone to future work, this is quite excellent. I'm happy to see this particular genre of game get more entires of this quality, and I'll be keeping an eye on this developer.

Highly recommended.

This game is short around 3-4 hours, but it's very memorable. Reminds me of Orwell (the first one, which was just amazing).

The interface is retro and stilted, but you can tell that it's a design choice by the author. Behind the retro graphics of what is essentially a conspiratorial work simulator, the game stands out as a very polished experience. I have experienced no bugs. Once I knew the basic game mechanics, I didn't feel cheated in anyway by the game. If I made a mistake during gameplay, it was because I was distracted, not because the game didn't provide enough clues.

The polish of the game also stands out with the brilliant sound design. The music is spot-on with some Tool-like guitars like the song Rosetta Stoned blended with futuristic suspense tunes.

Moreover, the game has its audio cues timed to the millisecond; they don't feel like jump scares but like actual sound design choices. The audio cues ALWAYS enhance the experience in this game, which was fascinating to experience.

The twists can be bland, but you still end up wanting to know more about the story. The first thing I did after finishing the game was checking out if a sequel is planned.

PS: I am a scientist by education and I was thrilled to see that the developer researched science and some real-life conspiracy history in surprising depth.

The Good:

- The simulated computer UI is slick and responsive, and very immersive (so long if you suspend disbelief that technology was this advanced in the early 90s lol).
- The soundtrack perfectly sets the mood.
- Most of the connections between clues are interesting and fun to figure out.
- The story is engaging and well-paced.

The Bad:

- The game is too short! Most of my other points are variations of this complaint.
- Not enough cases/clues, so the central mystery builds extremely quickly.
- Some tools you use only once.
- The ending is rather abrupt and either downbeat or an annoying cliffhanger, depending on your perspective.
- Player choice is largely an illusion. Depending on choices, some events play out slightly differently and a tiny bit more of the backstory is revealed or not, but 95% of the story is identical, including the ending.
- Voice acting is fine, but not amazing
- All this feels like a hook for a (hopefully larger and longer) sequel

All in all though, the quality of what IS in the game plus its low price moves it to the recommend column for me. It is up to you if a game you can beat in a sitting or two is worth whatever price it is at the moment. For me, it was.

I love cyber sleuthing games with my favorites being Orwell, Cyber Manhunt, and Her Story. So this definitely scratched an itch for me.

Forewarned the story is short with most of the negative reviews highlighting that. While I wouldve liked to have had more, I will say that I prefer games being straight to the point rather than needless filler. You can get maybe 3 hours out of this so if that is not worth 14 dollars for you, then maybe skip this.

Aside from the usual info gathering, the puzzles are thoroughly challenging with my favorite being a bomb defusal segment that I found to be quite challenging. But in a fun way. I wouldve liked to use the tools more like the bomb defusal and chemical analyzer more than once. It wouldve added another layer of challenge to the game.


I would definitely recommend buying and experiencing this game whether it be on sale or not.

First and foremost, I really enjoyed the characters, dialogue, puzzles, and story. I saw many comments saying that the twist was unexpected and, after having played the game myself, I'm going to have to agree that I ALSO did not see that coming! 

I feel it is worth mentioning that, one of the more unforgiving elements of this game is that you are unable to save and restart at the beginning of a chapter/day. Therefore, if you miss an achievement, you have to start the game all over again. This brings me to the next unforgiving aspect of this game which is that no dialogue or cut scene is skippable or able to be fast-forwarded (e.g. clicking to make dialogue scroll faster). 

Despite the fact that these elements made the game a little more frustrating, I welcome the challenge. It doesn't take away from my positive review nor my recommendation for others to check this game out. If anything, it makes the achievements feel earned. Additionally, the game is not very long. So, a few restarts shouldn't lock the player into an unrelenting commitment of innumerable hours. I put just 6.5 hours into the game and, to put my point into perspective, I restarted the game twice -- to get all 13 achievements.

The finale is also very unsatisfying, dissapointing and will leave your mouth dry.

For me, the game overall is 8.5/10, 100% worth playing.

This is a well executed game with a quality UI and sound design. My only criticism is that the developers took a lot of care into designing the game's computer mechanics but then do not give you very many opportunities to use them. I was looking forward to a puzzle solving/detective type experience where I could piece together clues and solve cases, however the game's story quickly takes center stage; just as the tutorial section of the game ends, and you think that you'll now get to work on a wide variety of cases, you come to realize the entire game is more or less a guided experience through a conspiracy story. 

I personally was hoping for a more subtle, open-ended experience that focused on case solving, where the conspiracy itself could be discovered by a clever player gradually and then pursued as a personal choice. What is offered is entertaining and engaging, but those looking for a good detective experience will be somewhat disappointed.

review_text_raw:
It's probably the best "PC Detective" game I've played. The puzzles make logical sense, the UI is clean, the story is mostly very good, especially in the first half, and the game doesn't hold your hand too much. The game is good at creating a tense, anxious atmosphere, and the blurry first-person scenes are also a really interesting creative choice that I enjoyed.

But it's got some pretty noticeable flaws. While most of the plot twists land successfully, the biggest reveal is very obvious by the time it arrives, and is not as shocking as the game thinks it is. The ending is rushed and unsatisfying. The VO performances range from competent to dreadful, and the script needed an editor to polish the clunky dialogue. And, most egregiously, none of your choices matter, which is always massively disappointing.

Overall, 7/10. If they make a sequel, I'll probably play it.
